name: Leadstart SSO for OpenID Connect
author: Leadstart

sections.description:
The plugin is an addon to the OpenID Connect Generic plugin which authenticates a user on each site.

Single sign-on. The plugin performs an OpenID Connect authorization against your provider. If the provider session exists, the visitor is signed in with no click and no password prompt.

Single logout. If you logout on a site you are logged out of them all. This happens through a signed top-level redirect chain that visits each configured site in turn and
ends at your provider’s end-session endpoint.

Roles and sign-on

By default, silent authentication is disabled for administrators to prevent the exploitation of hijacked provider sessions; however, administrators can still sign in by clicking. If your organization requires administrators to be signed in silently as well, you can modify this behavior using the LS_SSO_BLOCK_SILENT_ROLES constant (configured as a comma-separated list of role slugs, or left empty to permit all roles). Alternatively, you can utilize the ls_sso_block_silent_roles filter.

Requirements

  • The OpenID Connect Generic plugin, active and configured, on every participating site.
  • An OpenID Connect provider (Auth0, Keycloak, Okta, Entra ID and others).
  • HTTPS on every site.
sections.installation:
1. Install and configure OpenID Connect Generic on every site first, and
    confirm that signing in works on each one individually.
  2. Install and activate this plugin on every site.
  3. Generate one shared secret, to be used by all sites:
    php -r “echo bin2hex(random_bytes(32)), PHP_EOL;”
    The plugin’s settings screen also has a Generate button that produces one
    in your browser without sending it to any server.

  4. Configure each site, either in wp-config.php (preferred) or under
    Tools > Leadstart SSO > Settings if you cannot edit that file.
    LS_SSO_PEERS lists the other sites, so it differs per site, the secret and
    the store are identical on all sites:

    define( ‘LS_SSO_SECRET’, ‘your-64-character-hex-secret’ );
    define( ‘LS_SSO_PEERS’, ‘https://second-site.com,https://third-site.com’ );
    define( ‘LS_SSO_STORE’, ‘https://store-site.com’ );

    Sites may mix the two methods as long as the secret matches.

  5. Visit Tools → Leadstart SSO and run Test peers on each site.

  6. In OpenID Connect Generic, enable Alternate Redirect URI, then re-save
    Settings → Permalinks. Register each site’s /openid-connect-authorize URL
    with your provider.
sections.faq:
Where should the shared secret live?

In wp-config.php, if you can edit. A signing key in the options table is in every database backup and every export handed to a contractor, and is reachable by any vulnerability that discloses options.

If you cannot edit that file, many managed hosts allow plugin installation and no file access at all, set it under Tools > Leadstart SSO > Settings instead. The option is encrypted with sodium, using a key derived from the site’s security keys in wp-config.php, so a copy of the database alone does not reveal it. It is stored with autoload off and is never displayed again after saving. If the site’s security keys change, the plugin reports that the secret cannot be decrypted, and you enter it again. A constant, when defined, always wins and the field becomes read-only.

The screen shows a short fingerprint of the secret, so you can confirm every site holds the same value. When the fingerprints match, the secrets match; a mismatch explains the 403 errors.

What do the status codes mean?

The status code is the diagnosis, and these are unrelated:

  • 404 — no REST route on that site, so the plugin is not installed or not activated.
  • 503 — the plugin is installed but has no secret or is not configured yet.
  • 403 — the request was signed, received, but refused.

You have to work through the sites in order: install and activate on every site, then configure and test.

Can I mix wp-config.php constants and the Settings tab across sites?

Yes, each site resolves each setting independently: the constant if one is defined, the stored option otherwise. A site with file access can use constants while another uses the Settings screen, as long as the secret matches, compare the fingerprints to confirm.

Do all sites need the same plugin version?

They interoperate across versions: the signing format, headers and logout tickets have not changed since 1.0.0, but the REST routes moved in 1.1.0, so sites on 1.1.0 or later only connect to each other. Running the same version everywhere is still recommended, because newer versions add local behavior (for example, refusing silent sign-on for administrators) that only applies where installed.

Can I install it in mu-plugins on some sites and as a normal plugin on others?

Yes, per site. What you must not do is install it in both places on the same site: the classes then load twice from two paths, which is a fatal error. The plugin detects this, stops loading, and shows an admin notice naming the file that is actually running.

How do I deactivate the plugin if it stops the site from working?

Open https://your-site.com/wp-admin/?leadstart_sso_oidc_deactivate=1 and sign in as an administrator if asked. On that page the plugin loads none of its other files, so the page still opens when the plugin is causing errors elsewhere. Select Deactivate to switch it off. The address is the same on every site.

Can I run this on a host with no SFTP access?

Yes, every setting can be entered on the Settings tab. The plugin only needs to be installable and able to make outbound HTTPS requests.

What role do new users get?

Whatever Settings > General > New User Default Role says on that site, normally subscriber. OpenID Connect Generic does not set a role when it creates the account, so wp_insert_user() falls back to that option. Changing the setting is usually the whole answer; no code is needed.

In order to decide the role per user instead, use the ls_sso_map_roles filter. The plugin runs on every SSO login, including when no role claim is configured:

add_filter( 'ls_sso_map_roles', function ( $roles, $incoming, $user ) {
    return in_array( 'staff', $incoming, true ) ? array( 'editor' ) : array( 'customer' );
}, 10, 3 );

Administrators are never reassigned by this filter, so a misconfigured provider cannot demote a user.

If you map from a provider claim, note that Auth0 silently drops custom claims namespaced under an Auth0 domain — auth0.com, webtask.io and webtask.run are all rejected as namespaces. Please use a domain you control. A claim namespaced to your-tenant.auth0.com never arrives, and role mapping then appears broken with no error.

Does this work with WordPress Multisite?

The plugin is built for the opposite case: separate installations with separate databases. A multisite network already shares users, sessions and logout through WordPress core, and does not need this plugin.

What happens when a peer site is offline?

All updates are queued and retried with backoff, using Action Scheduler when available and WP-Cron otherwise.

Does SSO redirect every visitor, including search engines?

No, crawlers are excluded, the check runs at most once per browser per 30 minutes, and by default the check is performed in the browser rather than as a server-side redirect, so it cannot be captured by a page cache.

What personal data does this store?

The plugin stores no personal data of its own. The activity log records the event type, the peer site, the route, a WordPress user ID, and success or failure and never request bodies, meta values, tokens, or signatures. Rows are deleted automatically after 30 days, filterable via ls_sso_log_retention_days.

When uninstalling the plugin, it removes the log table entirely.
sections.changelog:
1.1.0

  • Renamed the plugin to Leadstart SSO for OpenID Connect. The REST routes moved to leadstart-sso-for-openid-connect/v1, so update every site at the same time.
  • Fixed the links to the Status, Settings and Activity tabs on the plugin’s screen.
  • Removed the order history shortcode ([cross_site_orders] and [leadstart_orders]) and the REST endpoint that served it.
  • A shared secret saved on the Settings tab is now stored encrypted with sodium, using a key derived from the site’s security keys.
  • The status screen reports when a stored secret cannot be decrypted, and whether the site’s security keys are defined in wp-config.php.
  • Added a deactivation page that works even when the plugin is causing errors: /wp-admin/?leadstart_sso_oidc_deactivate=1.
  • Fixed a fatal error when the plugin was installed both as a regular plugin and as a must-use plugin.

1.0.0

  • Initial release: SSO, single logout, order history.

short_description: The plugin provides a single sign-on, logout and signed cross-site connection for separate WordPress installs sharing one OpenID Connect provider.
